# How to use this {.unnumbered}

Everything from today is in here, including the parts we don't get to in the
room. Every grey box with a coral edge is a **prompt**: click the copy icon in its
corner, paste it into Claude Code or Codex, and change the bits in
\[square brackets\].

**The shape of the day:** the morning gets you running, has the agent do something
tedious for you, and then takes your paper apart. The afternoon blocks (sections
5–8) work in any order, today or next week.

| | Section | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| Morning | 1. Get it running | Claude Code or Codex, and git, working on your laptop |
| | 2. Do something tedious | A messy folder cleaned up, with a save point and an undo |
| | 3. What it knows about you | A profile that makes every answer fit you |
| | 4. Take a paper apart | Its biggest problem, and an attempt at a fix |
| Afternoon, pick | 5. Referee panel | Simulated referee reports, and an editor's letter |
| | 6. References | Searched, downloaded, DOI-checked, claim-checked |
| | 7. Leave a trail | A folder a co-author can rerun |
| | 8. Notes and structure | Where things go; a project file; notes the agent keeps |
| Any time | 9. Your own work | Starting points for next week |
| | 10. GitHub | A copy of the folder in the cloud; co-authors |
| | 11. Connectors | Your email, calendar and files, if you want them |

::: {.floor}
**Two rules for the day.** Don't overthink it: just use it. And when you get
stuck, ask the tool. *"How do I…?"*, *"What just happened?"*, *"Undo that."* It is
its own best manual.
:::

# Get it running

## What you need

**A paid subscription.** You only need one:

| If you pay for… | …install |
|---|---|
| **Claude** (Pro or Max) | **Claude Code** |
| **ChatGPT** (Plus, Pro, Business, Edu, Enterprise) | **Codex** |

Free plans don't work for either tool. BI's Gemini subscription doesn't either: it
can't touch the files on your computer. **No subscription today?** Pair up with
your neighbour, and sort one out tonight. One month of Claude Pro or ChatGPT Plus
is plenty to start.

**No admin rights needed** for the tools themselves; both install into your own
user folder. Git (step 5) may ask for admin rights, and there's a way around that.

## Install on Windows

**Step 1: open PowerShell.** Click **Start**, type `powershell`, and click
**Windows PowerShell**. Not the one ending in **(x86)**. You'll see a line like
`PS C:\Users\YourName>`. To paste into PowerShell, right-click in the window or
press **Ctrl+V**.

**Step 2: install your tool.** Paste **one** of these and press Enter.

Claude subscription (Claude Code):

```powershell
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path", [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path","User") + ";$env:USERPROFILE\.local\bin", "User")
```

Both lines, in one paste. The second puts `claude` on your PATH, so Windows can
find it. (No admin rights needed: it only changes your own settings.)

ChatGPT subscription (Codex):

```powershell
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.ps1 | iex"
```

Wait 1–3 minutes until the `PS C:\...>` prompt comes back. Then **close
PowerShell completely and open it again**. That step matters: it lets Windows find
the new program. Check:

```powershell
claude --version
```

(or `codex --version`). A version number means you're installed.

**Step 3: log in.** Type `claude` (or `codex`) and press Enter. Your browser opens:
log in with the account your subscription is on, approve, and go back to
PowerShell. Codex: choose **Sign in with ChatGPT**. You only do this once.

**Step 4: the test.** With the tool running, type a sentence:

```{.default .prompt}
What files are in this folder?
```

If it answers in plain English, **you're done**. To quit, type `/exit` (or press
**Ctrl+C** twice).

**Step 5: Git (everyone).** Git lets the agent save a snapshot before it changes
anything, so you can always go back. You'll use it from the first exercise on. You
never type git commands; you ask the agent. Quit the tool first (`/exit`), then:

```powershell
winget install --id Git.Git -e --source winget
```

Click **Yes** when Windows asks. Close PowerShell, open it again, and check with
`git --version`.

- **Can't click Yes (no admin rights)?** Start the agent and ask:

  ```{.default .prompt}
  Install the portable version of Git for Windows in my user folder, without admin rights, and put it on my PATH. Then check that git works in a new PowerShell window.
  ```

- **`winget` not recognized?** Download the installer from
  <https://git-scm.com/downloads/win> and click Next on every screen.

## Install on a Mac

Open **Terminal** (Cmd+Space, type `terminal`, Enter) and run one of these:

```bash
# Claude Code
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash

# Codex (needs Homebrew, from brew.sh)
brew install --cask codex
```

Then log in and test as in steps 3 and 4. For git, type `git --version`. If your
Mac offers to install the command line developer tools, click **Install**.

## If something goes wrong

Work down the list. The first two fix almost everything.

- **`claude` or `codex` is not recognized.** You skipped "close and reopen
  PowerShell". Open a fresh window and try again. Still failing? Run the install
  line again and watch for red text.
- **Claude Code: let it diagnose itself.** Run `claude doctor`. It often names the
  problem outright.
- **Codex stops and asks for administrator approval, or about a "sandbox".**
  Choose to continue **without** elevated setup (the restricted or "unelevated"
  mode). Codex works fine that way. This is what happened on BI laptops in August.
- **`irm` is not recognized.** You're in Command Prompt, not PowerShell. Open
  Windows PowerShell as in step 1.
- **The download fails, hangs, or says it's blocked.** That's BI's network or
  security software, not you. Put your hand up. For IT, the request is: *allow
  `claude.ai` and `downloads.claude.ai` (Claude Code) or `chatgpt.com` and
  `releases.openai.com` (Codex), and allowlist `claude.exe` / `codex.exe` in my
  user folder.*
- **Claude Code script blocked?** This often works instead:

  ```powershell
  winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode
  ```

- **"You need a paid plan", or login fails.** Check that you log in with the same
  account the subscription is on.

## The terminal on one page

Five commands and a few keys, all for moving around. Everything else, you ask the
agent to do.

| Type this | And it… |
|---|---|
| `cd foldername` | moves **into** a folder. `cd ..` steps back out. |
| `ls` | **lists** what's in this folder (`dir` also works on Windows) |
| `mkdir name` | **makes** a new folder |
| `pwd` | prints where you are |
| `explorer .` | opens this folder as an ordinary window (Mac: `open .`) |
| `claude` or `codex` | **starts the agent**, right here |

| Press | And it… |
|---|---|
| **Tab** | finishes a name: type the first letters of a folder, press Tab. It handles spaces in names. |
| **↑** | brings back your last command |
| **Ctrl+V** | pastes (right-click works too; Mac: **Cmd+V**) |
| **Ctrl+C** | stops whatever is running. Twice, or `/exit`, leaves the agent. |
| **Ctrl+L** | clears the screen |
| **Esc** | stops the agent mid-answer, so you can redirect it |

**Lost?** Close the window and open a new one; nothing breaks.

**Skip `cd`: open a terminal already in the right folder.**

- **Windows 11:** right-click the folder (or empty space inside it) → **Open in
  Terminal**.
- **Windows 10:** open the folder, click the address bar, type `powershell`, press
  Enter.
- **Mac:** drag the folder onto the Terminal icon in the Dock. (Right-click →
  **New Terminal at Folder** works too, once you switch it on in System Settings →
  Keyboard → Keyboard Shortcuts → Services.)
- **Anywhere:** type `cd ` (with a space) and drag the folder into the terminal
  window. It types the path for you.

This is the everyday move: open the folder, open a terminal in it, type `claude`.

## First contact

Make a practice folder, look at it, and start the agent in it:

```powershell
mkdir practice
cd practice
explorer .
claude
```

`explorer .` opens the folder you're in as an ordinary window (Mac: `open .`).
It's a normal folder: anything you drag into it, the agent can see.

(or `codex`). Then:

```{.default .prompt}
What files can you see here? Do not change anything.
```

::: {.floor}
**The floor:** ask it to make a file, read it back to you, and delete it again.
Done? You've used an AI agent on your own machine.
:::

If you're early, find the edge. Pick whatever tempts you:

- **Something from finance.**

  ```{.default .prompt}
  Price a European call with S = 100, K = 105, r = 4%, sigma = 20%, T = 1. Show the code and run it.
  ```

- **Watch it build something.** *"Write a small program that does X, and run it."*
  It doesn't just describe; it does.
- **Try to catch it out.** Something very recent, an obscure figure, a specific
  citation. Then **check** the answer.
- **Be vague on purpose.** *"Make me something useful for my course."* Does it ask
  you questions, or charge ahead?

Write down one answer that **surprised** you, and one you **didn't trust**, and why.

## Which model, and your limits

| | Claude Code | Codex |
|---|---|---|
| **Good** | **Opus**, Fable | **Sol**, Astra |
| **Fast** | Sonnet, Haiku | Luna |

- Use **Opus** (Claude Code) or **Sol** (Codex) by default. Fable and Astra are
  stronger still, and very expensive: they eat your limit fast.
- **Fast** models are for massive amounts of repetitive, easy work. **Luna is very
  cheap.** Haiku is cheap, but not at Luna's level.
- Switch with `/model` in either tool.

**Usage limits.** Every answer costs computing power; the strong models and long
thinking cost the most. **Claude Pro** runs out sooner within a five-hour window;
**ChatGPT Plus** runs out sooner over a week. Higher plans give many times more.

- **What eats it:** long sessions, big files, the strongest model, long thinking.
- **See where you stand:** `/usage` in Claude Code, `/status` in Codex.
- **Hit the limit?** Wait for the reset, switch to a Fast model, or pair up. If you
  keep hitting it, a higher plan is the fix.

## Talk instead of type

Speech-to-text makes long prompts painless, and long prompts get better answers.

- **Windows:** press **Windows key + H** in any text field, including PowerShell.
- **Mac:** press **Fn** twice (or the microphone key). Turn it on under System
  Settings → Keyboard → Dictation if nothing happens.

## Working safely

- **It works where you start it.** Start it in a project folder, not your whole
  Documents folder.
- **It asks before it does anything big.** Read before you say yes. Ask for a plan
  first: *"Tell me what you'd do. Don't change anything yet."*
- **Work on a copy** of anything precious, and use git (section 2) for save points.
- **What it reads is sent to the AI company.** Treat it like uploading to a cloud
  service. Keep out personal data (students, interview subjects) and confidential
  material.
- **Tired of approving every step?** Codex: run `codex --full-auto`, which stops
  asking but stays inside its sandbox. Claude Code: **Shift+Tab** to "accept
  edits", which approves edits in the folder but still asks before anything else.

# Save points (git)

Git records the history of a folder: every change, when, and why. Almost all
software is built with it (Linus Torvalds wrote it in 2005, for Linux), and here
it is **mainly for the agent**. The agent can change 40 files in 30 seconds; git
lets it, and you, see exactly what changed, and put it all back in one step. You
never type a git command. You ask.

**It isn't OneDrive.** OneDrive and Dropbox keep old versions of each file, saved
automatically. Git saves the whole folder at once, when you say so, with a note
saying why. OneDrive is a backup; git is a lab notebook. Keep both, but keep git
projects outside folders that OneDrive syncs.

## Your first save point

In your `practice` folder (section 1), with the agent running:

```{.default .prompt}
Set up git here. My name is [your name], my email is [your email].
```

```{.default .prompt}
Make a file notes.md with one line about my research. Commit it.
```

```{.default .prompt}
Add a second line.
```

```{.default .prompt}
What changed since the last commit?
```

## Undo

```{.default .prompt}
Revert to the last commit.
```

The second line is gone. Then:

```{.default .prompt}
Show me the history.
```

One word to be careful with: *revert **to** the last commit* goes back to it;
*revert the last commit* undoes that commit itself.

Done early?

```{.default .prompt}
Make a branch called experiment, add a line there, then switch back to main. Where did the line go?
```

## Keep things out: .gitignore

`.gitignore` is a file that lists what git should never save. The usual
candidates: personal data (interviews, anything with names or e-mail addresses),
passwords and keys, big files, other people's PDFs, and junk files (Word's `~$`
lock files, `.DS_Store`, `Thumbs.db`). Two things worth knowing:

- **Ignore before the first commit.** Once something is committed, it's in the
  history.
- **Ignored by git is not hidden from the agent.** It can still read those files.

## Exercise: a research project

`founders-study` is a made-up study of founders who change direction: interviews,
a survey, papers, a draft. Nothing in it is real. About ten minutes.

```{.default .prompt}
Download https://github.com/JonasMoss/vibing/raw/main/courses/2026-10-strategy/props/founders-study.zip into this folder and unzip it.
```

(Or unzip `practice/founders-study.zip` from the course files yourself.)

```{.default .prompt}
Go into founders-study. Set up git, but don't commit yet. Tidy the folders the way a researcher would, and show me the plan first.
```

```{.default .prompt}
Write a .gitignore. Explain each line in plain words.
```

```{.default .prompt}
Commit. What did git leave out, and why?
```

Then check:

```{.default .prompt}
If I pushed this to GitHub, would anything private go along?
```

## Five words, and how to ask about the rest

| Word | Means | You say |
|---|---|---|
| **commit** | a save point, with a note | *"Commit this."* |
| **revert** | undo: back to a save point | *"Revert to the last commit."* |
| **remote** | the copy elsewhere, usually GitHub | *"Is there a remote?"* |
| **push** | send your commits to the remote | *"Push."* |
| **pull** | fetch new commits from the remote | *"Pull."* |

The agent will use more words than these: repo, diff, branch, merge, origin,
main, worktree, pull request. You don't need to learn them. When one turns up,
ask:

```{.default .prompt}
What's a [word]? Two sentences, for a professor.
```

## GitHub and GitHub Pages

GitHub keeps your git history online, as your **remote**. It's owned by
Microsoft, and free, private repositories included. It's for backup, co-authors,
replication packages (Zenodo archives a GitHub release and gives it a DOI), and
web pages: **GitHub Pages** turns a folder into a web page, free for public
repositories. This course's page, vibing.jonasmoss.com, is one.

```{.default .prompt}
Publish this folder as a web page with GitHub Pages.
```

Setting up GitHub, co-authors and pull requests: section 11.

# Do something tedious

A messy folder, on your own machine: the job a chat window can't do, because it
can't touch your files.

The folder is an exam export, the way it comes out of WISEflow: 15 group
submissions in folders named like `[3-2048892] - Group 1`, each with a cover sheet
and an "Appendix material" folder full of files called `EKSAMEN.pdf`, `final.pbix`
or `dashboard_v3_FINAL.pbix`, plus an empty grade sheet in a different order from
everything else. It's synthetic, so nothing real is at risk.

::: {.floor}
**The floor:** the folder is reorganised and committed, and you've undone one
change with git.
:::

## Get it, and save a point

In your `practice` folder:

```{.default .prompt}
Download https://github.com/JonasMoss/vibing/raw/main/courses/2026-10-finance/props/decrap-me.zip into this folder and unzip it.
```

Then, **before it changes anything**:

```{.default .prompt}
Set up git here and commit everything.
```

The first time, git needs your name and email:

```{.default .prompt}
Set up git with my name, [Your Name], and my email, [you@bi.no].
```

Now it can't do anything you can't undo. Note the order: a save point taken
*after* the mess is a save point of the mess.

## Clean it up

```{.default .prompt}
What's in decrap-me? What would annoy a teacher about it? Don't change anything.
```

```{.default .prompt}
Reorganise it so I can grade quickly: one folder per group, files named by group and what they are, and the grade sheet sorted by group. Show me the plan first.
```

**Argue with the plan.** Change at least one thing: the folder names, what happens
to the cover sheets, whatever you'd do differently. Then *"Go ahead."*

```{.default .prompt}
Make a grading table: group, participant ID, report file, dashboard file, and an empty column for the mark.
```

## What changed, and the undo

```{.default .prompt}
What changed since the last commit?
```

Every move and rename, listed. Then *"Commit."* Now be bold:

```{.default .prompt}
Delete the Marking guidance folder.
```

Gone? Then:

```{.default .prompt}
Go back to the last commit.
```

It's back. **Save point first, then courage.** That's the habit for every folder you
care about: commit, let it try, look at what changed, keep it or go back.

What git is, and the words for it: section 2.

# What it knows about you

## What it can see

The agent only knows what's in its **context window**: your profile, the project
file in this folder, this conversation, and the files it has opened. Nothing else.
`/clear` empties the conversation and everything it read. Your profile and the
project file load again.

**Try it.** Tell it one thing about yourself, for example what you teach. Type
`/clear`. Then ask: *"What do you know about me?"*

## Who is asking?

Without context, it answers **the typical person who would type your question**.
*"Can I deduct my home office?"* gets US tax rules unless you say you work in
Norway. A specialist is far from typical, so the default answer is aimed at someone
else.

The demo from the room: *"A: 48 purchases from 1,000 visitors. B: 62 from 1,000.
Is B better?"* With no profile, a cautious frequentist answer (p ≈ 0.17). With
*"I'm a Bayesian statistician; I read Gelman, Jaynes and McElreath"*, a 91% chance B
is better: ship it. With the single line *"My intellectual idol is Jim Berger"*,
Claude reached for Sellke, Bayarri and Berger (2001) and said there's at least a
45% chance of no real difference. **One line changed the school.**

You can't opt out of being stereotyped. You can choose the stereotype.

## Does it matter in your field?

In statistics, in the terminal, it barely matters. Fields with schools of thought
may be different. Find out with your neighbour:

```{.default .prompt}
Is the value premium compensation for risk, or mispricing?
```

Ask it once with no profile. Then add one line to the folder's `AGENTS.md`:
one of you writes *"I'm in the Fama–French tradition"*, the
other *"I work in behavioural finance; I read Shiller and Thaler."* Type `/clear`,
ask again, and compare. Other questions that split schools: *"Do active funds beat
index funds after fees?"*, *"Is momentum a risk factor?"*

## Your profile: how you work

What reliably carries across every project is **how you work**: the rules you're
tired of repeating. For example:

- *I work in R* (or Stata, or Python).
- *Cluster standard errors by firm unless I say otherwise.*
- *I write in LaTeX. Never give me Word unless I ask.*
- *Tell me what you'll do before you change anything.*

## Two files

| | About | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Your profile** | You: how you work, your field and school | `.claude\CLAUDE.md` or `.codex\AGENTS.md` in your home folder |
| **Project file** | This folder: the paper, the data, the rules | `AGENTS.md` in the folder (both tools) |

Your profile is read in every project; a project file only in its own folder. Both
are plain text you can open in Notepad.

## Exercise: write your profile

1. Two sentences on **who you are**: your field, your school, what you read.
2. Three **rules** you'd give any research assistant: your tools, your style, one
   pet peeve.
3. Ask:

   ```{.default .prompt}
   Save these as my personal profile, the file you read in every project: [your sentences and rules]
   ```

   Claude asks permission first, because the file is outside this folder.
4. Test it in a fresh folder: ask for something your rules should change. Did they
   stick?
5. *"Open my profile in Notepad."* (Mac: TextEdit.) That's all it is.

**Codex users: write more than one line.** In testing, Codex ignored one-line
profiles that Claude picked up.

**Homework.** Talk for 90 seconds with speech-to-text about how you work and who you
are, then *"Add this to my profile."* Keep adding: corrected it twice about the same
thing? It goes in. In the **chat apps**, the "who you are" half matters most; put it
in custom instructions.

# Take a paper apart

Pick a recent paper, let the agent read all of it, find its biggest problem, and
ask it to fix it. Finding a hole worth working on usually takes weeks of reading.
Here it takes a minute, and you spend your time judging.

::: {.floor}
**The floor: one problem you have checked against the paper yourself.** A fix that
holds up is the bonus.
:::

## Get a paper

Pick a **recent paper in your field**: one you know well (so you can judge the
answers), or one you've been meaning to read. Make a folder for it and start the
agent there:

```powershell
mkdir paper
cd paper
claude
```

- **Open PDF link** (NBER, arXiv and similar):

  ```{.default .prompt}
  Download this paper into this folder: [paste the link]
  ```

- **SSRN or a journal website** usually blocks the agent. Download the PDF in your
  browser, then:

  ```{.default .prompt}
  Move the PDF I just downloaded into this folder.
  ```

If it says it can't read the PDF, tell it to find a way. It may ask to install a
small tool; say yes.

## Ask

Talk to it like a colleague who has just read the paper.

```{.default .prompt}
What's the main claim here?
```

Check this against your own reading. If it gets the claim wrong, everything after
it is suspect.

```{.default .prompt}
What's the biggest methodological problem?
```

```{.default .prompt}
Can you fix it?
```

A theory paper or a case study works too: the problem may be an assumption, the
sample, or the evidence behind the main result.

## Push

The first answer is rarely the best one.

- *"Show me where in the paper."* Every claim should come with a quote. Find it in
  the paper yourself; it takes seconds.
- *"Do they address it anywhere, including the appendix?"* A first critique is often
  already answered in the paper. This is the push people skip.
- *"Is that really the biggest problem?"*
- *"That's generic. What's specific to this paper?"*
- *"Show that the fix works."* It may write and run a simulation, or fetch public
  data.

A fix takes **5–10 minutes**: it writes and runs code. Let it work. If it asks to
install Python, say yes.

**Then:** try it on your own working paper, before a referee does. **Keep the
folder**: everything in the afternoon starts from it.

# Referee panel

Who will referee your paper, and what will they say? Find out before you submit.

Real referees read your paper cold, alone, each with their own hobby-horses. A
fresh session of the agent knows nothing but the paper and what you give it, so
**one fresh session per referee** gives you independent reports. And names carry a
lot: *"as Campbell Harvey would"* brings the factor zoo and the t > 3 bar with it.

```{=html}
{{< include decks/images/referee-panel.svg >}}
```

::: {.floor}
**The floor: two referee reports from fresh sessions, and one concern in them you
hadn't thought of.**
:::

## Who would referee this?

In your paper folder:

```{.default .prompt}
Who are the five most likely referees for this paper, judging by its references? One line each: what would they care about?
```

Argue with the list. Add the one you fear most.

## Ask how it's done

The most underused move with these tools: **ask the agent how a job should be done
before you ask it to do it.**

```{.default .prompt}
I want simulated referee reports on this paper. How does a good finance referee work? How deep should they go? Should they try to reproduce the main results? Propose a procedure.
```

Argue with it, then:

```{.default .prompt}
Save what we agreed as reviews/how-to-referee.md.
```

## One fresh session per referee

Type `/clear`, so the next referee starts cold, with only the paper and the
procedure. Then:

```{.default .prompt}
Referee this paper as [name] would, following reviews/how-to-referee.md. Save it as reviews/[name].md.
```

Repeat for each referee, with `/clear` before each.

**In a hurry?** Run them side by side: open a second PowerShell window in the same
folder and start another `claude` or `codex` there. Claude Code can also do it in
one prompt: *"Run the referees as parallel subagents."*

## Not what you wanted?

**Change the procedure, not the report.** Tell the agent, or edit
`reviews/how-to-referee.md` in Notepad:

- *Go deeper on identification.*
- *Try to reproduce Table 2.*
- *Check whether the data are available.*
- *One page. No summary of the paper.*

Then `/clear` and rerun. If you'll do this for every paper, make the procedure a
skill (section 9):

```{.default .prompt}
Turn reviews/how-to-referee.md into a skill called referee-panel.
```

## The editor

`/clear`, then:

```{.default .prompt}
You're the editor. Read the reports in reviews/. Where do the referees agree, where do they disagree, and what must be fixed before submission?
```

Then the useful bit:

```{.default .prompt}
Draft a plan for each must-fix concern: new analysis, rewriting, or an argument.
```

## Worth knowing

- Use it on **your own paper**, before a real referee does. A published paper is
  fine for practice.
- Different tools and different runs find different problems. Compare with your
  neighbour, or run Claude and Codex on the same paper.

# References

Four jobs, one prompt each. Do them in any order, on your paper's reference list or
your own draft.

::: {.card}
**Why bother.** An audit of 2.5 million biomedical papers found fabricated
references in **1 in 277** papers in early 2026, up from 1 in 2,828 in 2023
(Topaz et al., *The Lancet*, 2026; a letter, and its method has been questioned).
Closer to home: a 2026 paper in *Structural Equation Modeling* cites Foldnes &
Grønneberg (2024), and the DOI resolves to a 2022 "Editorial acknowledgement". The
paper reports simulation results for methods from a source that doesn't exist.

The models got better; the practice didn't. A current model **with search**
doesn't invent DOIs. Its failures now are the wrong paper, or a paper it couldn't
fetch, and both take seconds to catch.
:::

## Search

Shallow and deep are two different requests, not two settings.

**Shallow: one specific question.** The trick is to be specific. Mine, in a field I
know well:

```{.default .prompt}
What's similar to Hjort–Glad density estimation with a parametric start? Other kernel estimators with something that could count as a parametric start, also on domains other than the real line? Do any outperform it? Download the papers into literature/, and give me the DOI for any you can't get.
```

Questions like this keep turning up important papers I didn't know existed. Yours:

```{.default .prompt}
What's similar to [your idea, in one exact sentence]? Has anyone built something like it? Does it beat [the usual approach]? Download the papers into literature/, and give me the DOI for any you can't get.
```

*"Papers on [your topic]"* gets you the famous ones you already know. A specific
question gets you the one you missed.

Also quick: pinning down a paper you half-remember.

```{.default .prompt}
Find the actual paper: full citation, all authors, journal, year and DOI. [what you remember]. If you can't find it, say so. Don't guess.
```

**Deep: every paper.** You're finalizing, not exploring: the related-work section,
a grant application, a referee response.

```{.default .prompt}
I need every method since [year] related to [your idea]: working papers too, and other names for the same idea. Make a table: paper, what it does, how it relates to mine. Take your time.
```

It's slow, and it uses a good part of your usage limit. Start it, then get coffee.

## Keep the papers in the folder

The habit that makes everything else here work: every paper you need sits in the
project folder, so the agent reads the paper itself instead of searching for it
again, or relying on its memory of it. Make it a rule in the project file
(section 9), once:

```{.default .prompt}
Add to the project file: papers go in literature/. Whenever we need one, download it there if you can get it. If you can't, give me the DOI so I can.
```

Catching up on a paper you've already written:

```{.default .prompt}
Do that for every paper in my reference list. Put the DOIs you couldn't get in literature/to-fetch.md.
```

- Paywalls stop it, and BI's library takes the DOI list.
- SSRN blocks agents. Download in your browser, then *"Move it into literature/."*
- Using git? *"Keep literature/ out of git."* Track the text you wrote, not the PDFs
  you downloaded.

## DOI check

```{.default .prompt}
Check every entry in the reference list. Does the DOI resolve to this exact paper: same title, authors and year? Make a table: OK, wrong paper, no DOI, not found. Fix what you can, and tell me how you know.
```

Then check three yourself: paste each DOI after `https://doi.org/`. Same paper?

**Practice file.** A messy `.bib` handed over by a fictional co-author, with six
planted traps (a DOI that points to the rebuttal, a sequel that was never written,
and so on), plus two warm-up files. Ask the agent:

```{.default .prompt}
Download https://github.com/JonasMoss/vibing/raw/main/courses/2026-10-finance/props/references-practice.zip into this folder and unzip it. Then read messy-list.bib and do what the comment at the top says.
```

## Claim check

The one nobody does: **does the cited paper say what it's cited for?** This is where
the literature folder pays off: the papers are already there, so it quotes the real
text instead of searching for it.

```{.default .prompt}
Take each citation in the introduction. Read the cited paper in literature/ and check whether it supports the sentence it is cited for. Quote the passage. Make a table: sentence, citation, supports / partly / doesn't / not in the folder, quote.
```

- Run it on **your own draft** before you submit.
- "Not in the folder" is not "doesn't exist". Get those through the library, put
  them in literature/, and ask again.

**A polished bibliography is not evidence of a correct bibliography.**

# Leave a trail

Turn a messy project into something a co-author could rerun, and check that they
could. Practice on a messy one first, then do the same with a copy of one of your
own folders.

::: {.floor}
**The floor: the rerun test passes.** After `/clear`, the agent reruns your folder
from scratch and gets the same numbers.
:::

## The folder

A paper you're writing with Kari Nordmann (fictional): *Monthly or yearly? Price
framing and willingness to pay.* A survey experiment, cleaned by hand in Excel,
analysed twice and written up in Word. Start the agent in an empty folder and ask:

```{.default .prompt}
Download https://github.com/JonasMoss/vibing/raw/main/courses/2026-10-finance/props/messy-project.zip into this folder and unzip it.
```

What you get:

```
messy-project/
├── survey_export_2026-03-14.csv    the raw survey, 240 rows
├── data_clean_FINAL.csv            cleaned by hand in Excel
├── analysis.py                     first try
├── analysis_v2.py                  the analysis
├── table1.txt                      results
├── table1 (copy).txt               results?
├── notes.txt                       "the crazy WTP ones?? ask Kari"
└── draft_v3.docx                   the Word draft
```

Could Kari rerun this? Could you, next spring?

## Organise

First a save point, the same move as in section 2:

```{.default .prompt}
Set up git here and commit everything.
```

Then:

```{.default .prompt}
Organise this folder so a co-author could rerun everything. Show me the plan first. Don't move anything yet.
```

Argue with the plan: folder names, where the raw data goes, what happens to old
versions. Nothing should be deleted; old versions can get a folder of their own.
Then *"Go ahead."*

```{.default .prompt}
Write a README for a co-author, and a project file for you. Then commit.
```

The **README** is for people: what this is, and how to rerun it. The **project
file** (`AGENTS.md`) is for the agent, which reads it every time it
starts here.

## The test

Type `/clear`. The agent now knows nothing about this folder, like a new co-author.

```{.default .prompt}
Rerun everything from scratch. Do you get the same numbers?
```

Not the same, or it can't? That's the useful part:

```{.default .prompt}
What's missing? Fix it, so the next rerun works.
```

Using the practice folder? Compare the rerun with the numbers in the Word draft.
They don't match, and finding out why is the point of the exercise.

## Why text

| | Invisible | Visible |
|---|---|---|
| **Writing** | Word: you can't see what changed | Text: every change shows |
| **Data** | Clicking in Excel: no record | A script: the steps are the record |

Writing in LaTeX? That's text already. Writing in Word? Keep Word for the paper,
keep the rest in text, and ask for a Word copy when you need one: *"Make a Word copy
of README.md."*

You may remember Reinhart and Rogoff's "Growth in a Time of Debt" (2010): above
90% debt to GDP, average growth of −0.1%. In 2013 a graduate student, Thomas
Herndon, couldn't reproduce it, asked for the spreadsheet, and got +2.2%. Part of
the gap was an `AVERAGE` over the wrong rows, which left out five countries; the
rest was years left out and the weighting. Your own rerun finds that kind of thing
first. **A wrong script you can read beats a
right click you can't remember.**

# Notes and structure

Where things go, and how the agent keeps track of a project for you.

## Four questions

Answer these about a real project, in your own words:

1. What do you re-explain **every single time**? → that goes in the project file.
2. Where does **undone work** live? (If the honest answer is "my head" or "my
   inbox", that's the finding.) → a to-do file.
3. Where are you **allowed to be wrong**? → notes, drafts, scratch.
4. What could you **never rebuild**? → raw data, the manuscript. Protect it.

Everyone already has a filing system. It just isn't written down, so it can't be
delegated to a co-author or an agent.

## An example: my paper folder

Every paper of mine starts like this (a skill sets it up):

```
my-paper/
├── AGENTS.md       the rules, for the agent
├── README.md       for people: what this is, how to rerun it
├── STATUS.md       where we are, what's next
├── manuscript/     everything that ends up in the PDF
├── code/           everything that computes
├── results/        the numbers the paper relies on
├── dev/            notes, drafts, talks: in git, not published
└── local/          downloaded papers, raw runs: not in git
```

My four answers: the project file (`AGENTS.md`), `STATUS.md`, `dev/`, and
`manuscript/` with `results/`. Yours will look different, and that's the point of
the next step.

**`dev/` or `local/`?** Both hold things that aren't the paper. The difference is
git:

| | In git and on GitHub | Published with the paper |
|---|---|---|
| `manuscript/`, `code/`, `results/` | yes | yes |
| `dev/` | yes | no |
| `local/` | no | no |

- **`dev/`** is work in progress: notes, drafts, talks. It's committed, so it's
  backed up on GitHub and your co-authors see it, but it never goes out with the
  paper.
- **`local/`** is listed in `.gitignore`, a plain-text file that tells git which
  files and folders to leave alone. Git never sees them, so they never reach
  GitHub: downloaded PDFs you may not redistribute (in `local/literature/`), big
  raw files, anything else that stays on your machine. To set it up: *"Keep local/
  out of git."*

## Ask for a structure, not a template

```{.default .prompt}
Here is how I work: [your four answers]. Propose a folder structure for this paper and a project file that says where things go. Show me first; don't move anything.
```

Argue with it. Then *"Go ahead"*, and *"Commit"* if you use git. Check nothing got
lost: *"How many files were there before, and how many now?"*

## Notes the agent keeps for you

```{.default .prompt}
At the end of each session, add what we did and what's next to notes/log.md. Put this rule in the project file.
```

```{.default .prompt}
Keep literature/notes.md: one paragraph per paper we read, with the pages that matter.
```

Next time you sit down:

```{.default .prompt}
Read the project file and the log, then tell me where we left off.
```

## The project file

A plain-text file in the folder that the agent reads at every start: what the
project is, where things go, and your rules. Your profile is about *you*; the
project file is about *this folder*.

**One file: `AGENTS.md`.** Codex and Claude Code both read it. One catch: if the
folder also has a `CLAUDE.md`, Claude Code reads that instead, so keep just the one
file. Both tools also read project files in the folders above where you start them,
so start the agent in the project folder itself.

**Getting one, and changing it.** You don't write it yourself; you ask:

```{.default .prompt}
Write an AGENTS.md for this folder: what the project is, where things go, and the rules you should follow. Show me first.
```

Changes go the same way: *"Add to AGENTS.md: never edit anything in data/raw."*
Then read what it wrote: the first draft describes the folder, but only you know
the rules. (`/init` drafts one too. In Claude Code it writes a `CLAUDE.md`, so ask
for `AGENTS.md` by name instead.)

**What goes in:**

- what this is, in one paragraph: the paper, the question, the data;
- where things go: *raw data in data/raw, papers in literature/, scripts in code/,
  the paper is LaTeX in paper/*;
- the rules: *never edit anything in data/raw; download papers into literature/,
  and give me the DOI when you can't; only cite references with a verified DOI*;
- how to rerun everything, in one command.

**Keep out** what it can see for itself (the file list), long essays, passwords,
and anything about you (that's your profile).

**The habit that pays off.** Corrected it twice about the same thing? Then:

```{.default .prompt}
Add that to the project file.
```

Every correction you write down is one you never make again. Keep it short: it's
read at every start. It's plain text, so open it in Notepad and fix it yourself
whenever it's wrong.

## Skills, if you're curious

> Memory is the AI remembering you. A skill is you writing it down.

A **skill** is a saved workflow with a name and a note on when to use it. It's worth
making one for a routine you **repeat**, want done **the same way every time**, or
want to **hand to a colleague**. You never touch the file format; you ask:

```{.default .prompt}
Turn what we just did into a skill called tidy-paper.
```

From then on, *"tidy this paper"* runs the whole routine. Most things work fine
without skills. Only bother for the ones you catch yourself repeating.

# Your own work

Bring the real thing. Commit first (*"Set up git here and commit everything"*),
then let it try.

- A replication, with public data:

  ```{.default .prompt}
  Get the Fama–French factors from Ken French's website and reproduce the summary statistics for RM−RF, SMB and HML in Table 2 of Fama and French (1993), July 1963 to December 1991. Then extend it to today: does it still hold?
  ```

- A project folder: *"What's here? What's missing? What would you do first?"*
- A dataset: *"Describe this data. What looks odd?"*
- A draft: *"Where is the argument weakest?"*
- A referee report you received: *"Draft a response plan, point by point."*
- A course: *"Turn my lecture notes into exercises with solutions."*
- A lecture animation, like the compound-interest one from the morning:

  ```{.default .prompt}
  Make a 15-second animated SVG that explains [compound interest] to first-year students. Three scenes, one caption each.
  ```

  It's one file that plays in any browser. Change a number or a caption and ask again.
- Anything you've been putting off because it's tedious.

**Before you leave: what will you try on Monday?** Pick one thing, and put it in
your calendar. And don't overthink it: just use it.

## Worth reading

- **[Epoch AI benchmarks](https://epoch.ai/benchmarks)**: where to track what the
  models can do.
- **[One Useful Thing](https://www.oneusefulthing.org/)**, Ethan Mollick: the
  best running account of using these tools for academic work.
- **[The Plain Person's Guide to Plain Text Social Science](https://kieranhealy.org/files/papers/plain-person-text.pdf)**,
  Kieran Healy. Written for social scientists, not programmers.
- **[Good enough practices in scientific computing](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005510)**,
  Wilson et al. (2017). For researchers who aren't software engineers.
- **[Spreadsheet horror stories](https://eusprig.org/research-info/horror-stories/)**,
  EuSpRIG. Real incidents with price tags.

Questions afterwards: jonas.moss@bi.no

# GitHub, if you want it

**git** is the save points on your laptop (section 2). **GitHub** is a copy of
that folder, with all its save points, in the cloud. It survives a dead laptop,
lets a co-author work on the same folder, and records every change with a date and
a name. OneDrive keeps files in sync; GitHub keeps every version.

**Why a researcher might want it:** backup with history; co-authors on one folder
instead of emailed attachments; replication packages (journals increasingly ask
for code and data, and a GitHub repository archived on [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org)
gets a DOI); course pages built from plain text.

## Set up, once

1. Make a free account at <https://github.com>. Private repositories are free.
2. Ask the agent:

   ```{.default .prompt}
   Install the GitHub command-line tool and log me in.
   ```

   It installs `gh` and opens your browser to log in.

## Put a folder on GitHub

```{.default .prompt}
Put this folder on GitHub as a private repository called [name]. Check .gitignore first: no PDFs, no raw data, nothing confidential.
```

Then, whenever you've committed something worth keeping:

```{.default .prompt}
Push my latest changes.
```

**Laptop dead?** On the new one, ask: *"Download my repository [name] into this
folder."* Everything is back, with its whole history.

## Working with a co-author

- You: *"Add [their GitHub username] as a collaborator."*
- They: *"Download [the repository link] into this folder."*
- Every session: *"Pull the latest changes."* Work. *"Commit and push."*
- Both edited the same file? *"Merge our changes and show me what you did."*

## Pull requests

Instead of pushing straight into your project, a co-author can **propose** a
change: a pull request. You read it, discuss it, and accept it (merge) or not. The
discussion and the revisions stay attached to the change. It's referee-and-revise,
for a folder.

**Their side:**

```{.default .prompt}
Make a new branch, [the change], commit it, push it, and open a pull request to [owner] that explains what you changed and why.
```

**Your side:**

```{.default .prompt}
Are there open pull requests on this repository? Summarise them.
```

```{.default .prompt}
Check out the pull request and test it. Does everything still run? Do any numbers change?
```

Then *"Comment on the pull request: [your question]"*, or *"Merge it, then pull
the latest changes."*

## Exercise: in pairs

Both of you need a GitHub account and the GitHub tool (see "Set up, once"). Any
folder works; the practice folder from section 3 already has its history.

1. **A:**

   ```{.default .prompt}
   Put this folder on GitHub as a private repository called [name], and add [B's GitHub username] as a collaborator.
   ```

2. **B:**

   ```{.default .prompt}
   Accept the GitHub invitation from [A's username], and download [A's username]/[name] into this folder.
   ```

   (The invitation also arrives by email, if the agent can't find it.)

3. **B:**

   ```{.default .prompt}
   Make a new branch, [your change], commit it, push it, and open a pull request that explains what you changed and why.
   ```

4. **A:** *"Any open pull requests? Summarise them."* Then comment, or merge.
5. Swap roles.

## Keep an eye on it

- **GitHub tells you.** Click **Watch** on the repository's page, and you get an
  email (or a push notification in the GitHub mobile app) for every new pull
  request.
- **Claude Code, while it's open,** can check on a timer:

  ```{.default .prompt}
  /loop 10m check for new pull requests on this repository, and summarise any new ones.
  ```

- **A reviewer on GitHub itself.** Connect the Claude or Codex app to the
  repository once. Then comment `@claude` or `@codex review` on a pull request,
  and it posts a review there.

## Public or private

- **Private by default.** Only you and the people you invite can see it.
- **Public** only for what you'd publish anyway: a replication package, a course
  page.
- **History is forever.** A file you delete later is still in the history, so
  never commit passwords, student data or confidential data in the first place.
- **Research data:** check the data agreement before it goes to any cloud service.

# Connectors: email, calendar, files

**MCP** is a standard plug that lets the agent use other services: your email,
calendar or files, the same way it uses your folder. Each plug is called a
**connector**.

**Switch one on (Claude).** Go to `claude.ai/customize/connectors`, pick **Gmail**,
**Google Calendar** or **Google Drive**, click **Connect**, and approve with your
Google account. Start a new Claude Code session and type `/mcp`: it's in the list.
Codex supports MCP too; ask it how to connect yours.

**Email:**

```{.default .prompt}
Find all my emails from [name] this month. One line each: date, subject, what they want.
```

```{.default .prompt}
Draft a reply. Show it to me before you send it.
```

**Calendar:**

```{.default .prompt}
What does my week look like? Find two free hours for writing, and put them in my calendar.
```

**Drive:**

```{.default .prompt}
Find the referee report on [paper] in my Google Drive, and draft a response plan, point by point.
```
